paragraphs: One circumstance struck Grigory particularly, and it confirmed a very unpleasant and revolting suspicion. This Lizaveta was a dwarfish creature, “not five foot, within a wee bit,” as many of the pious old women said of her pathetically after her death. Her broad, healthy, red face had a look of blank idiocy, and the fixed stare in her eyes was unpleasant, in spite of their meek expression. She wandered about summer and winter alike, barefoot, wearing nothing but a hempen smock. Her coarse, almost black hair curled like lamb’s wool and formed a sort of huge cap on her head. It was always caked with mud and had leaves, bits of stick and wood shavings clinging to it, because she always slept on the ground, in the dirt. Her father was a homeless, sickly drunkard called Ilya. He had lost everything and lived for many years as a workman with some well-to-do tradespeople. Her mother had long been dead. Spiteful and diseased, Ilya used to beat Lizaveta inhumanly whenever she came back to him. But she rarely did, because everyone in the town was ready to look after her, as an idiot who was therefore especially dear to God. Ilya’s employers, and many others in the town, especially among the tradespeople, tried to clothe her better. They always rigged her out with high boots and a sheepskin coat for the winter. But although she let them dress her up without resisting, she would usually go off, preferably to the cathedral porch. There she took off everything she had been given—kerchief, sheepskin, skirt or boots—left it all there and walked away barefoot in her smock as before. On one occasion a new governor of the province, making a tour of inspection of our town, saw Lizaveta and was wounded in his tenderest feelings. He was told she was an idiot, but he declared that for a young woman of twenty to wander about in nothing but a smock was a breach of decency, and must not happen again. But the governor went on his way, and Lizaveta was left as she was. At last her father died, which made her even more acceptable in the eyes of the religious people of the town, as an orphan. In fact, everyone seemed to like her. Even the boys didn’t tease her, and the boys of our town, especially the schoolboys, are a mischievous lot. She would walk into strange houses, and no one drove her away. Everyone was kind to her and gave her something. If she was given a copper, she would take it and at once drop it into the alms-jug of the church or the prison. If she was given a roll or a bun in the market, she would hand it to the first child she met. Sometimes she would stop one of the richest ladies in the town and give it to her, and the lady would be pleased to take it. She herself never tasted anything but black bread and water. If she went into an expensive shop where costly goods or money were lying about, no one kept watch on her. They knew that even if she saw thousands of roubles left unguarded, she wouldn’t touch a farthing. She hardly ever went to church. She slept either in the church porch or over a hurdle (there are many hurdles instead of fences in our town to this day) in some kitchen garden. About once a week at least she turned up “at home,” that is, at the house of her father’s former employers, and in winter she went there every night and slept either in the passage or the cowhouse. People were amazed that she could stand such a life, but she was used to it, and although she was so tiny, she had a robust constitution. Some of the townspeople said she did all this out of pride, but that is hardly credible. She could hardly speak and only now and then let out an inarticulate grunt. How could she have been proud?

It happened one clear, warm, moonlit night in September (many years ago). Five or six drunken revelers were coming home from the club at a very late hour, by our provincial standards. They went by the “back-way,” which ran between the back gardens of the houses, with hurdles on either side. This way leads out onto the bridge over the long, stinking pool that we were used to calling a river. Among the nettles and burdocks under the hurdle, the revelers saw Lizaveta asleep. They stopped to look at her, laughing, and began joking with unbridled coarseness. One young gentleman took it into his head to ask, as a whimsical question, whether anyone could possibly look on such an animal as a woman, and so forth.... They all declared, with lofty disgust, that it was impossible. But Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was among them, sprang forward and declared that it was by no means impossible, and that there was, in fact, a certain piquancy about it, and so on.... It’s true that at that time he was overdoing his part as a buffoon. He liked to push himself forward and entertain the company, ostensibly on equal terms, of course, though in reality he was on a servile footing with them. It was just when he had received the news of his first wife’s death in Petersburg. With crape on his hat, he was drinking and behaving so shamelessly that even the most reckless among us were shocked at the sight of him. The revelers laughed, of course, at this unexpected opinion, and one of them even began challenging him to act on it. The others rejected the idea even more emphatically, though still with the utmost hilarity, and at last they went on their way. Later on, Fyodor Pavlovitch swore that he had gone with them, and perhaps it was so. No one knows for certain, and no one ever knew. But five or six months later, the whole town was talking, with intense and sincere indignation, about Lizaveta’s condition, and trying to find out who was the scoundrel who had wronged her. Then suddenly a terrible rumor went all over town that this scoundrel was none other than Fyodor Pavlovitch. Who set the rumor going? Of that drunken band, five had left the town. The only one still among us was an elderly and much respected civil councilor, the father of grown-up daughters, who could hardly have spread the tale, even if there had been any foundation for it. But rumor pointed straight at Fyodor Pavlovitch, and kept on pointing at him. Of course this was no great grievance to him. He wouldn’t have bothered to contradict a set of tradespeople. In those days he was proud, and didn’t condescend to talk except in his own circle of officials and nobles, whom he entertained so well.

At the time, Grigory stood up for his master vigorously. He provoked quarrels and arguments in his defense and succeeded in bringing some people round to his side. “It’s the wench’s own fault,” he insisted, and the culprit, he said, was Karp, a dangerous convict who had escaped from prison. His name was well known to us, because he had hidden in our town. This guess sounded plausible, for it was remembered that Karp had been in the neighborhood just at that time in the autumn and had robbed three people. But this affair and all the talk about it did not turn popular sympathy away from the poor idiot. She was better looked after than ever. A well-to-do merchant’s widow named Kondratyev arranged to take her into her house at the end of April, meaning not to let her go out until after the confinement. They kept a constant watch over her, but in spite of their vigilance she escaped on the very last day and made her way into Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. How she managed, in her condition, to climb over the high, strong fence remained a mystery. Some maintained that somebody must have lifted her over. Others hinted at something more uncanny. The most likely explanation is that it happened naturally: Lizaveta, used to clambering over hurdles to sleep in gardens, had somehow managed to climb this fence in spite of her condition, and had leapt down and hurt herself.

Grigory rushed to Marfa and sent her to Lizaveta, while he ran to fetch an old midwife who lived close by. They saved the baby, but Lizaveta died at dawn. Grigory took the baby, brought it home, and made his wife sit down and put it on her lap. “A child of God—an orphan is kin to everyone,” he said, “and to us above all. Our little lost one has sent us this child, who has come from the devil’s son and a holy innocent. Nurse him and weep no more.”

So Marfa brought up the child. He was christened Pavel, and people were quick to add Fyodorovitch (son of Fyodor). Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t object to any of this and thought it amusing, though he kept vigorously denying that he was responsible. The townspeople were pleased that he had taken in the foundling. Later on, Fyodor Pavlovitch invented a surname for the child, calling him Smerdyakov, after his mother’s nickname.

So this Smerdyakov became Fyodor Pavlovitch’s second servant, and he was living in the lodge with Grigory and Marfa when our story begins. He worked as the cook. I ought to say something about this Smerdyakov, but I am ashamed to keep my readers’ attention so long on these common menials, and I will go back to my story, hoping to say more of Smerdyakov as it goes on.
